AI.method: Systematic X-ray spectral analysis of 27 GRGs using archival XMM-Newton and Chandra observations, including spectral fitting to derive absorption, line, and continuum parameters, plus comparisons with extended radio power and black hole mass estimates.
AI.result: 44% show intrinsic absorption (N_H,int ≥ 10^21 cm^-2); several show narrow Fe Kα lines (EW up to ~570 eV); soft X-ray thermal plasma (kT~0.2–0.8 keV) and ionized absorbers/outflows common; hard photon indices (median Γ~1.6); many sources have strong X-ray cores relative to lobes; a positive M_BH–L_2-10 keV trend found, no clear Eddington ratio–mass dependence, and a tentative negative λ_Edd–Γ trend.
AI.conclusion: GRGs exhibit diverse nuclear conditions and accretion states. Their properties support scenarios where obscuration, episodic/restarted activity, and low-efficiency accretion collectively shape long-term GRG evolution. Larger samples are needed to confirm the preliminary accretion relations.

title: Revealing the Physical Driver of the Baldwin Effect: Gas Density in the Broad-Line Region
comment: Comments: 11 pages, 7 figures, 4 appendix figures. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The Baldwin effect --- the inverse correlation between the equivalent width of emission lines and the continuum luminosity in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) --- has been known for nearly five decades, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. Using a sample of 41,159 radio quasars constructed from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Low-Frequency Array Two-metre Sky Survey, we investigate the origin and underlying physics of the Baldwin effect of MgII broad emission lines in both radio-quiet (RQ) and radio-loud (RL) quasars. We find that the slope $β$ of the Baldwin effect is positively correlated with the Eddington ratio $λ_{\rm Edd}$ in both populations, and RL quasars exhibit steeper $β$ than their RQ quasars at fixed $λ_{\rm Edd}$. Photoionization simulations reveal that the $β$ is primarily governed by the gas density in the broad-line region (BLR): lower gas densities yield steeper slopes. This density-driven mechanism naturally connects the Baldwin effect to the broader AGN evolutionary context. Specifically, higher $λ_{\rm Edd}$ drive stronger accretion disk winds, leading to denser BLRs and shallower $β$. Our findings indicate that BLR gas density serves as the primary physical driver underlying the "global" Baldwin effect, offering a physically grounded framework for interpreting AGN accretion states and their coupled evolution with host galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the physical origin of the Baldwin effect (inverse correlation between emission-line equivalent width and continuum luminosity) in MgII broad emission lines using 41,159 radio quasars from SDSS and LoTSS. The authors find that the Baldwin effect slope β correlates positively with Eddington ratio, with radio-loud quasars showing steeper slopes than radio-quiet ones at fixed Eddington ratio. Photoionization simulations reveal that the slope is governed by broad-line region (BLR) gas density—lower densities yield steeper slopes—establishing gas density as the primary physical driver of the "global" Baldwin effect.
AI.motivation: The Baldwin effect has been known for nearly five decades, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. This paper aims to uncover the underlying physics driving this empirical correlation between emission-line strength and continuum luminosity in AGNs.
AI.method: The study uses a large sample of 41,159 radio quasars from SDSS and LoTSS, separating them into radio-quiet and radio-loud populations. The authors measure the Baldwin effect slope β for MgII emission lines and correlate it with Eddington ratio. They complement their observational analysis with photoionization simulations to isolate the physical parameters controlling the slope, particularly focusing on BLR gas density and its connection to accretion disk winds.
AI.result: The Baldwin effect slope β is positively correlated with Eddington ratio in both radio-quiet and radio-loud quasars. Radio-loud quasars exhibit steeper slopes than radio-quiet quasars at fixed Eddington ratio. Photoionization simulations show that lower BLR gas densities produce steeper slopes, indicating gas density is the primary controlling parameter.
AI.conclusion: BLR gas density serves as the primary physical driver of the "global" Baldwin effect. Higher Eddington ratios drive stronger accretion disk winds, producing denser BLRs and shallower slopes. This density-driven mechanism connects the Baldwin effect to AGN evolutionary context, offering a physically grounded framework for interpreting AGN accretion states and their coupled evolution with host galaxies.

title: The SRG/eROSITA All-Sky Survey DR2: Cumulative X-ray catalogues from the first three surveys and multi-wavelength counterparts in the western Galactic hemisphere
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A. Accompanying eROSITA-DE Data Release 2
summary: The eROSITA telescope array on board the Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission began its all-sky survey program in December 2019, scanning the sky at an approximately six-month cadence. Here, we present new catalogues of point-like and extended X-ray sources derived from the first three completed eROSITA all-sky surveys (eRASS:3), covering the western Galactic hemisphere, which Germany's eROSITA consortium holds proprietary rights for. We describe the observational strategy, data processing, and analysis pipelines. We also characterise the resulting X-ray source populations. The eRASS:3 main catalogue contains nearly two million sources, including 1,911,744 point-like and 63,796 extended sources, detected in the 0.2-2.3 keV energy band, eROSITA's most sensitive energy window. This volume has doubled the X-ray source content of eRASS1 and provides a comprehensive census of X-ray-emitting objects across diverse astrophysical classes. We also released a secondary hard catalogue of nearly 15,000 sources detected in the harder 2.3-5.0 keV energy band. In addition, we released six catalogues, three for the main sample and three for the hard sample, in which we identify and classify the optical and infrared counterparts of eRASS:3 point-like sources. This approach delivers a homogeneous, high-quality identification of mostly extragalactic X-ray emitters; for example, we estimate that approximately 88% of the 1.4 million counterparts identified within the footprints of the Legacy Survey Imaging for DESI are extragalactic sources. This work has enabled the generation of samples optimised for completeness and purity, while expanding the discovery space for rare populations. The second data release (DR2) of the SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey is a catalogue-only release, comprising the catalogues presented in this work together with an updated version of the eROSITA upper flux limit server.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the eRASS:3 catalogue, derived from the first three eROSITA all-sky surveys covering the western Galactic hemisphere. It contains nearly 2 million sources (1,911,744 point-like and 63,796 extended) in the 0.2-2.3 keV band, plus a hard-band catalogue of ~15,000 sources in 2.3-5.0 keV, along with six optical/IR counterpart catalogues. These constitute the SRG/eROSITA second data release (DR2).
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive census of X-ray-emitting objects across diverse astrophysical classes by doubling the X-ray source content of the previous eRASS1 release, and to deliver homogeneously classified counterpart catalogues that enable studies optimized for completeness and purity while expanding discovery space for rare populations.
AI.method: The work describes the observational strategy of eROSITA's all-sky survey (six-month cadence starting December 2019), data processing and analysis pipelines, and generation of both main (0.2-2.3 keV) and hard (2.3-5.0 keV) band catalogues. Optical and infrared counterpart identification and classification are performed for point-like sources, using surveys such as the Legacy Survey Imaging for DESI, resulting in six counterpart catalogues (three for main, three for hard samples).
AI.result: The eRASS:3 main catalogue contains 1,911,744 point-like and 63,796 extended sources, nearly doubling the eRASS1 source content. The hard catalogue contains nearly 15,000 sources. Approximately 88% of the 1.4 million counterparts identified within DESI Legacy Survey footprints are estimated to be extragalactic. The release (DR2) also includes an updated eROSITA upper flux limit server.
AI.conclusion: This catalogue-only DR2 release of the SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey delivers a large, homogeneously processed dataset of X-ray sources with high-quality counterpart identifications, providing a robust foundation for X-ray astronomy research across diverse astrophysical classes.

title: The eROSITA X-ray luminosity function of active galactic nuclei
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures. Catalogue including redshift information is released via the eROSITA web pages and CDS upon the journal's article acceptance
summary: The X-ray luminosity function (XLF) of active galactic nuclei (AGN) provides an observational probe of the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) across cosmic time. With its large survey grasp, Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA samples the luminosity--redshift plane with a depth--area balance complementary to pencil-beam surveys, providing the volume needed to detect rare luminous AGN, previously limited by small-number statistics. We measure the soft XLF, leveraging an eROSITA sample spanning approximately eight orders of magnitude in luminosity out to $z\simeq6$. This enables us to study luminosity-dependent evolution with improved constraints, and to infer both the SMBH accretion history and optical/UV missed AGN population. We introduce a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterisation in which all XLF model parameters are allowed to evolve continuously with redshift. We find lower space densities for moderately and very luminous AGN at low redshift, while the abundance is higher than previously found at the highest redshifts. Comparisons to optical/UV quasar LFs converted to rest-frame $2\!-\!10\,\mathrm{keV}$ show that the UV-missed fraction decreases with luminosity, and, in the most luminous bin, increases with redshift. Integrating the XLF yields a black-hole accretion-rate density peaking at $z \simeq 1.5$, with the corresponding cumulative black-hole mass density indicating $\sim80^{+11}_{-23}\%$ obscured growth relative to locally-inferred BH mass estimates derived from scaling relations and missed by the soft X-ray selection of our sample. With this work, we release the eROSITA DR2 AGN catalogue, including counterparts and their redshift information. We then discuss how these results can inform future spectroscopic, photometric, and X-ray survey strategies aimed at improving AGN demographic constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the soft X-ray luminosity function (XLF) of AGN using SRG/eROSITA data spanning ~8 orders of magnitude in luminosity out to z~6, introducing a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterization. It finds lower space densities of luminous AGN at low redshift but higher abundances at high redshift, constrains the UV-missed AGN population, and derives a black-hole accretion-rate density peaking at z~1.5 with ~80% obscured growth. The eROSITA DR2 AGN catalogue is also released.
AI.motivation: The soft XLF of AGN is a key observational probe of SMBH growth across cosmic time, but previously limited by small-number statistics for rare luminous AGN. eROSITA's wide survey provides the depth-area balance needed to measure the XLF with improved constraints on luminosity-dependent evolution, the SMBH accretion history, and the population of AGN missed by optical/UV selection.
AI.method: The authors leverage an eROSITA sample spanning ~8 orders of magnitude in luminosity out to z~6 and introduce a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterization in which all XLF model parameters evolve continuously with redshift. They measure the soft XLF, compare it to optical/UV quasar luminosity functions, integrate it to derive the black-hole accretion-rate density and cumulative BH mass density, and release the eROSITA DR2 AGN catalogue.
AI.result: They find lower space densities for moderately and very luminous AGN at low redshift, while abundances are higher at the highest redshifts than previously found. The UV-missed fraction decreases with luminosity and increases with redshift in the most luminous bin. The BH accretion-rate density peaks at z~1.5, and the cumulative BH mass density implies ~80^{+11}_{-23}% obscured growth relative to local BH mass estimates.
AI.conclusion: The eROSITA XLF provides improved constraints on AGN demographics and evolution, revealing the UV-missed AGN population and quantifying the extent of obscured SMBH growth. The released DR2 catalogue and findings inform future spectroscopic, photometric, and X-ray survey strategies for improving AGN demographic constraints.

title: Thermal or Non-thermal? Diffuse emission in the infall region of stacked galaxy groups
comment: Submitted to A&A, 12 pages, 5 figures, 1 table
summary: The faint infall regions surrounding the virial radius of galaxy groups remain largely unexplored due to their low X-ray surface brightness. Using the large statistical power of SRG/eROSITA survey observations, we present the first spectroscopic measurement of the intragroup medium (IGrM) in the infall regions of a large sample of low-mass galaxy groups ($M_{\rm tot}<1\times10^{14}\,M_{sun}$), extending to $\sim2\,R_{200m}$ (2.2 Mpc). Through spectral stacking of 827 nearby groups from the first eROSITA All-Sky Survey catalog, we detect diffuse emission and measure the thermodynamic properties of gas at densities previously inaccessible to X-ray observations. The stacked spectra are well described by a Gaussian differential emission measure model, yielding a temperature distribution with a mean temperature of $0.96_{-0.04}^{+0.05}$ keV and width of $0.28_{-0.10}^{+0.10}$ keV, and a metal abundance of $0.21_{-0.04}^{+0.06}$ A$_{sun}$, consistent with expectations for group outskirts. The inferred electron densities decrease from $(4.8\pm1.3)\times10^{-5}$cm$^{-3}$ at $(0.7-2)\,R_{500c}$ to $(5.5\pm2.0)\times10^{-6}$ cm$^{-3}$ at $(2-4)\,R_{500c}$, demonstrating eROSITA's ability to probe the low-density outskirts of galaxy groups. Residual emission in the spectra suggests the presence of an additional spectral component. While a secondary thermal interpretation requires an unexpectedly hot, metal-poor plasma, a non-thermal inverse Compton model provides an equally plausible explanation, contributing $\sim30\%$ of the thermal flux. Assuming that the additional component is produced by inverse Compton emission from a common population of relativistic electrons, the inferred magnetic field strength would be in the sub-$μ$G regime.

AI.tldr: Using SRG/eROSITA survey data, this study provides the first spectroscopic measurement of the intragroup medium in the infall regions of 827 low-mass galaxy groups out to ~2 R200m, detecting diffuse X-ray emission at unprecedented low densities and measuring temperature, abundance, and electron density profiles. Residual emission suggests an additional spectral component, possibly non-thermal inverse Compton emission implying sub-μG magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: The faint infall regions around the virial radius of galaxy groups are largely unexplored due to their low X-ray surface brightness. This work aims to fill this observational gap using the large statistical power of the SRG/eROSITA survey to probe gas properties in group outskirts at densities previously inaccessible to X-ray observations.
AI.method: Spectral stacking of 827 nearby low-mass galaxy groups (M_tot < 1e14 Msun) from the first eROSITA All-Sky Survey catalog. Stacked spectra were fit using a Gaussian differential emission measure model to extract thermodynamic properties, and the inferred electron density profile was derived as a function of radius relative to R500c.
AI.result: The stacked spectra yield a mean temperature of 0.96(+0.05/-0.04) keV, a temperature width of 0.28(+0.10/-0.10) keV, and a metal abundance of 0.21(+0.06/-0.04) Asun. Electron densities decline from (4.8±1.3)e-5 cm^-3 at (0.7-2) R500c to (5.5±2.0)e-6 cm^-3 at (2-4) R500c. Residual emission suggests an additional component—either an unexpectedly hot, metal-poor thermal plasma or a non-thermal inverse Compton emission contributing ~30% of the thermal flux, implying sub-μG magnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: eROSITA demonstrates its capability to probe the low-density outskirts of galaxy groups out to ~2 R200c (2.2 Mpc). The detection of a possible non-thermal component at sub-μG field strengths opens new avenues for studying relativistic electron populations and magnetic fields in the outskirts of low-mass structures, though the physical nature of the residual emission remains ambiguous.

title: Invariant manifolds in barred galaxy simulations. III. Self-regulated weakening of strong spiral arms
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in A&A on 30/07/2026
summary: We investigated the origin of the weakening of strong spiral arms in barred galaxies, seeking the physical mechanism responsible for the decline in the fraction of manifold-trapped particles over time. We reconstructed the gravitational potential of a fully self-consistent N-body simulation of a barred galaxy using AGAMA, computed the Lagrangian points, and quantified how their spiral-induced angular displacement affects the geometry of the invariant manifolds and the associated orbital flows. We find that sufficiently strong, self-gravitating spiral arms significantly reshape the gravitational potential of a barred galaxy, displacing the equilibrium points up to 20-50° from the bar major axis, where they are expected to lie in the standard invariant-manifold framework. This shift alters the configuration of the manifold branches and disrupts the coherent stellar flows that sustain the spiral structure. As the spiral weakens, the equilibrium points gradually return to their standard configuration, restoring the conditions for manifold-driven spiral arm formation on a timescale of ~200 Gyr. We show for the first time that invariant manifolds and the spiral structures they generate are coupled through a self-regulating feedback mechanism, allowing the spiral pattern to recur over time. Our results therefore indicate that, although barred galaxies may sustain spiral activity over long timescales, individual episodes of strong spiral arms are intrinsically transient.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why strong spiral arms weaken in barred galaxies by reconstructing the gravitational potential of an N-body simulation and analyzing Lagrangian points and invariant manifolds. The authors find that strong self-gravitating spirals displace equilibrium points by 20-50° from the bar major axis, disrupting manifold-driven stellar flows. As spirals weaken, equilibrium points return to standard positions on a ~200 Gyr timescale, revealing a self-regulating feedback loop between manifolds and spirals that makes individual spiral episodes transient while enabling long-term recurrence.
AI.motivation: To identify the physical mechanism responsible for the decline in the fraction of manifold-trapped particles and the weakening of strong spiral arms in barred galaxies over time.
AI.method: Reconstructed the gravitational potential of a fully self-consistent N-body simulation of a barred galaxy using AGAMA; computed Lagrangian equilibrium points; quantified how spiral-induced angular displacement affects invariant manifold geometry and orbital flows.
AI.result: Strong self-gravitating spiral arms displace Lagrangian points 20-50° from the bar major axis, altering manifold branch configurations and disrupting coherent stellar flows. Equilibrium points return to standard positions on a ~200 Gyr timescale as spirals weaken, demonstrating a self-regulating feedback loop between invariant manifolds and spiral structures.
AI.conclusion: Invariant manifolds and spiral structures are coupled through a self-regulating feedback mechanism allowing spiral recurrence over long timescales, but individual episodes of strong spiral arms are intrinsically transient.

title: Tidal Disruption Events with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/TaoAn03. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) and related nuclear transients probe jet launching, disk formation and circularization, particle acceleration, and the circumnuclear medium (CNM). However, the small fraction of events launching relativistic jets, the weak or delayed radio emission of many thermal TDEs, and the black-hole demographics of galactic nuclei remain poorly understood. SKA, with microJy sensitivity, wide bandwidth, long baselines, rapid response, and commensal surveys across 50-350 MHz (SKA-Low) and 0.35-15.4 GHz (SKA-Mid), will transform this field. Its sensitivity, frequency coverage, and very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) capability will extend radio calorimetry from a few well-studied nearby events to volume-limited samples of non-relativistic outflows. The SKA will bring off-axis and mildly relativistic jets into routine reach, trace CNM density profiles through the evolution of the low-frequency synchrotron turnover, and localize faint off-nuclear transients with sub-arcsecond precision. These data will constrain jet incidence, energetics, geometry, and magnetization, map the CNM through shock interactions, test links to changing-look active galactic nuclei (AGN) and high-energy neutrinos, and identify off-nuclear events associated with recoiling supermassive or intermediate-mass black holes. We discuss the benefits of commensal surveys, rapid triggering, and SKA-VLBI, and provide predictions based on the projected performance of AA* and AA4. SKA will shift TDE radio studies from detailed case-by-case studies to population-scale inference, advancing studies of jet physics and black-hole demographics.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), with its microJy sensitivity, wide bandwidth, rapid response, and VLBI capability, will transform tidal disruption event (TDE) radio studies from case-by-case analysis to population-scale inference, enabling routine detection of off-axis and mildly relativistic jets, mapping of circumnuclear medium densities, and advancing constraints on jet physics and black-hole demographics.
AI.motivation: Current understanding of TDEs is limited by the small fraction of events that launch relativistic jets, weak or delayed radio emission in many thermal TDEs, and poor understanding of black-hole demographics in galactic nuclei. Radio observations have only been possible for a few well-studied nearby events.
AI.method: The paper discusses SKA's technical capabilities (microJy sensitivity, 50-350 MHz SKA-Low and 0.35-15.4 GHz SKA-Mid bands, VLBI baselines, rapid triggering, commensal surveys) and provides predictions based on projected performance of AA* and AA4. It outlines observational strategies including radio calorimetry for volume-limited samples, low-frequency synchrotron turnover tracking, and sub-arcsecond localization of off-nuclear transients.
AI.result: The SKA will bring off-axis and mildly relativistic jets into routine reach, trace CNM density profiles through low-frequency synchrotron turnover evolution, constrain jet incidence, energetics, geometry, and magnetization, map the CNM via shock interactions, and identify off-nuclear events linked to recoiling supermassive or intermediate-mass black holes.
AI.conclusion: SKA will shift TDE radio studies from detailed case-by-case analyses to population-scale inference, transforming jet physics and black-hole demographics research.

title: A search for HI absorption in distant star-forming galaxies with ASKAP-FLASH - II. Direct observations and stacking of 21 cm line
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present results of a search for associated and intervening HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies and a control sample of radio galaxies at 0.4 < $z$ < 1.0, using ASKAP's FLASH HI 21 cm absorption survey. We report the detection of a new HI 21 cm absorption line in radio galaxy NVSS J214954-004657 at $z_{\mathrm{HI}}$ = 0.863. Additionally, we present results of HI 21 cm stacking for associated and intervening star-forming and radio galaxy catalogues. For the first time at these redshifts, we report tentative detections of stacked HI 21 cm absorption for associated galaxies when stacked in order of descending radio source brightness, and show that these tentative detections become buried as optical depth increases as progressively weaker sources are co-added into the stack. No stacked signal is detected when co-adding intervening galaxy spectra. We speculate that the ability to detect a stacked HI 21 cm detection is dependent on the background source optical depth limits, as well as source covering factors. Covering factor has a greater impact when stacking intervening systems, and can be considered to effectively weaken the observed flux density of a radio source. We find no significant difference in detection rate for associated HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies versus the general radio-source population at the same redshift. Although detection rates are low, from a meta-analysis of HI 21 cm surveys we find that 1 detection is expected given the survey parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a search for HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming and radio galaxies at 0.4 < z < 1.0 using ASKAP's FLASH survey. They detect one new HI 21 cm absorber in NVSS J214954-004657 at z=0.863, present tentative stacked detections for associated galaxies (which weaken as fainter sources are added), and find no detection when stacking intervening systems, attributing results to background source optical depth limits and covering factors.
AI.motivation: To investigate the presence and distribution of neutral hydrogen (HI) in star-forming galaxies and radio galaxies at intermediate redshifts (0.4-1.0), a regime poorly explored for HI 21 cm absorption, and to understand the detectability of such features via both direct detection and stacking techniques.
AI.method: The authors used ASKAP's FLASH HI 21 cm absorption survey to search for associated and intervening HI absorption lines toward star-forming galaxies and a control sample of radio galaxies. They conducted HI 21 cm stacking for both associated and intervening galaxy catalogues, including stacking in order of descending radio source brightness, and performed a meta-analysis of HI 21 cm surveys to compare detection rates against expectations.
AI.result: Detection of one new HI 21 cm absorption line in NVSS J214954-004657 at z=0.863. First-time tentative stacked detections for associated galaxies when stacked by descending radio brightness, which disappear as weaker sources are added (increasing optical depth). No stacked signal for intervening systems. No significant difference in detection rates between star-forming and general radio-source populations. The meta-analysis predicts 1 detection given the survey parameters, matching observations.
AI.conclusion: Stacked HI 21 cm absorption detection feasibility depends on background source optical depth limits and covering factors; covering factor significantly affects intervening systems by effectively reducing observed radio flux. Associated HI absorption detection rates in star-forming galaxies are consistent with the broader radio-source population at these redshifts, and the low detection rate is consistent with expected statistics.

title: Thermal Breaking of the I-Love Universality for Hot White Dwarfs
summary: The universal I-Love-Q relations for compact stars have significant applications in gravitational-wave astronomy, but thermal effects can break these relations in low-mass white dwarfs. In this work, we employ the stellar evolution code MESA to construct realistic models of $0.15 \, M_{\odot}$ helium-core and $0.6 \, M_{\odot}$ carbon-oxygen core white dwarfs at various temperatures. By utilizing the Clairaut-Radau equation, we quantitatively extract the radial variation of the eccentricity of internal isodensity surfaces. Our numerical results demonstrate that higher central temperatures amplify the eccentricity variation, causing the I-Love relations to deviate from the zero-temperature Chandrasekhar model, whereas subsequent cooling restores them. This confirms that the temperature-induced violation of the universal relations is fundamentally driven by the loss of self-similarity in isodensity surfaces, providing key insights into the applicability conditions of I-Love-Q relations in compact objects.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how thermal effects break the universal I-Love-Q relations in low-mass white dwarfs. Using the MESA stellar evolution code to model 0.15 M☉ helium-core and 0.6 M☉ carbon-oxygen core white dwarfs at various temperatures, the authors employ the Clairaut-Radau equation to extract eccentricity variations of internal isodensity surfaces. They find that higher central temperatures amplify eccentricity variation and cause deviations from the zero-temperature Chandrasekhar model, while cooling restores the universal relations, confirming that temperature-induced violations stem from loss of self-similarity in isodensity surfaces.
AI.motivation: The I-Love-Q relations are powerful tools for gravitational-wave astronomy, but their validity across different astrophysical conditions—particularly for white dwarfs where thermal effects may be significant—is not fully established. Understanding when and why these relations break down is crucial for correctly applying them in observational contexts.
AI.method: The authors use the MESA stellar evolution code to construct realistic models of low-mass white dwarfs (0.15 M☉ helium-core and 0.6 M☉ carbon-oxygen core) at various temperatures. They then apply the Clairaut-Radau equation to quantitatively extract the radial variation of eccentricity of internal isodensity surfaces within these models.
AI.result: The numerical results show that higher central temperatures amplify eccentricity variation in the isodensity surfaces, causing the I-Love relations to deviate from the zero-temperature Chandrasekhar model. Subsequent cooling restores compliance with the universal relations, confirming that temperature-induced violation of I-Love-Q relations is driven by the loss of self-similarity in isodensity surfaces.
AI.conclusion: The temperature-induced violation of universal I-Love-Q relations in low-mass white dwarfs is fundamentally caused by the loss of self-similarity in internal isodensity surfaces. This provides key insights into the applicability conditions of I-Love-Q relations for compact objects.

title: Angular Momentum Evolution from Core to Disk Scales in the Early Phase of Star Formation: Constraints from HH 212, HH 211, and B335
summary: I investigate the angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in the early phase of star formation using three protostellar systems: HH 212, HH 211, and B335. Observations show that the specific angular momentum follows a power-law dependence at core scales and transitions to an approximately constant value at smaller radii, indicating dynamical collapse in the inner envelope. I model this behavior using the inside-out collapse solution of Shu (1977) and its rotating extension, the Terebey-Shu-Cassen model, including modest magnetic effects through a flattened, magnetized core. I find that the observed angular momentum profiles in all three sources are broadly consistent with an inside-out collapse scenario with approximate conservation of specific angular momentum in the collapsing region. The inferred collapse ages and mass infall rates yield total masses accreted onto the center that are broadly consistent with the central masses derived from kinematics, allowing for a fraction of the material to be ejected by jets and winds. The predicted midplane densities at typical radii, including the effect of magnetic flattening, are also consistent with observational estimates. The three systems exhibit a similar pattern of angular momentum evolution despite large differences in the magnitude of their specific angular momentum. In particular, the small disk in B335 can be naturally explained by its lower initial specific angular momentum, although alternative explanations, such as magnetic braking or different initial conditions, cannot be excluded. These results suggest that inside-out collapse, with modest magnetic modification, provides a plausible first-order description of angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in the early phase of star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in three protostellar systems (HH 212, HH 211, and B335) and finds that the observed profiles are broadly consistent with an inside-out collapse scenario (Shu 1977; Terebey-Shu-Cassen model) with modest magnetic effects. The inferred collapse ages, infall rates, and predicted densities align with observations, and differences across systems (e.g., B335's small disk) are naturally explained by variations in initial specific angular momentum.
AI.motivation: To understand how angular momentum is transported and evolves from large cloud-core scales down to the much smaller disk scales during the early phases of star formation, using three protostellar systems as test cases.
AI.method: Analytical modeling of three protostellar systems (HH 212, HH 211, B335) using the Shu (1977) inside-out collapse solution and its rotating Terebey-Shu-Cassen extension, incorporating modest magnetic effects via a flattened, magnetized core. Observed angular momentum profiles are compared to model predictions for collapse age, mass infall rate, accreted mass, and midplane density.
AI.result: All three sources show angular momentum profiles consistent with inside-out collapse with approximate specific angular momentum conservation in the collapsing region. Inferred accreted masses match kinematically derived central masses (allowing for jet/wind ejection), predicted midplane densities with magnetic flattening agree with observations, and B335's small disk is naturally explained by its lower initial specific angular momentum.
AI.conclusion: Inside-out collapse with modest magnetic modification provides a plausible first-order description of angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in early star formation, though alternative explanations (e.g., magnetic braking, different initial conditions) cannot be fully excluded.

title: High-mass binary black hole mergers from detailed binary evolution models
summary:
Gravitational-wave observations reveal a population of binary black hole (BBH) mergers with primary masses above ${\sim}40\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, extending into and potentially beyond the pair-instability mass gap, with a possibly flat mass-ratio and broader χ_\mathrm{eff} distribution. We investigate whether super-Eddington accretion during stable mass transfer in isolated binary evolution can produce BBH mergers consistent with these properties across primary BH mass, mass-ratio, and χ_\mathrm{eff} distributions. Using POSYDON, we simulate BBH merger populations with primary BH masses above ${\sim}40\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, under three BH accretion efficiencies: Eddington-limited, GRRMHD-informed, and fully conservative. We additionally vary the natal kick strength, including strong kicks at high BH masses.
  We find that super-Eddington accretion does not suppress BBH mergers in the high-mass regime. Fully-conservative accretion leads to an increase of BBH mergers in POSYDON with a strong kick-independent peak at $χ_\mathrm{eff}=0.6$ and a sharp mass-ratio peak at $q\sim0.5$, whereas observations favor $χ_\mathrm{eff}=0.0$ and a flatter mass-ratio distribution. The GRRMHD-informed and Eddington-limited accretion are compatible with the observed primary BH mass and mass ratio distribution, but require natal kicks to populate negative χ_\mathrm{eff}.
  A joint analysis of the primary BH mass, mass ratio, and χ_\mathrm{eff} distributions provides strong constraints on binary evolution physics, and disfavor fully-conservative BH accretion as the dominant formation mechanism for high-mass BBH mergers. The Eddington-limited and GRRMHD-informed prescriptions with modest kicks can explain part of the high-mass population, but an additional formation channel is still needed to account for the high fraction of negative χ_\mathrm{eff} systems and high secondary BH spins.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether super-Eddington accretion during stable mass transfer in isolated binary evolution can explain observed binary black hole (BBH) mergers with primary masses above ~40 M⊙. Using the POSYDON population synthesis code, the authors test three BH accretion efficiencies (Eddington-limited, GRRMHD-informed, fully-conservative) and varied natal kick strengths. They find fully-conservative accretion produces a strong peak at χ_eff=0.6 and q~0.5, inconsistent with observations favoring χ_eff=0.0 and flatter mass ratios. The GRRMHD-informed and Eddington-limited prescriptions with modest kicks can partially explain the population, but an additional formation channel is still needed for negative χ_eff systems and high secondary spins.
AI.motivation: Gravitational-wave observations have revealed a population of high-mass BBH mergers (primary masses above ~40 M⊙) that extend into the pair-instability mass gap with possibly flat mass-ratio and broader spin (χ_eff) distributions. The authors aim to determine whether super-Eddington accretion during stable mass transfer in isolated binary evolution can produce BBH mergers consistent with these observed properties, providing constraints on binary evolution physics.
AI.method: Using the POSYDON population synthesis code, the authors simulate BBH merger populations with primary masses above ~40 M⊙ under three BH accretion efficiency prescriptions: Eddington-limited, GRRMHD-informed, and fully-conservative. They additionally vary the natal kick strength, including strong kicks at high BH masses, and jointly analyze the primary BH mass, mass-ratio, and χ_eff distributions.
AI.result: Super-Eddington accretion does not suppress high-mass BBH mergers. Fully-conservative accretion increases BBH merger rates but produces a strong kick-independent peak at χ_eff=0.6 and a sharp mass-ratio peak at q~0.5, inconsistent with observations favoring χ_eff=0.0 and a flatter mass-ratio distribution. The GRRMHD-informed and Eddington-limited prescriptions are compatible with observed mass and mass-ratio distributions but require natal kicks to populate negative χ_eff values. Joint analysis disfavors fully-conservative accretion as the dominant formation mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Fully-conservative BH accretion is disfavored as the dominant formation mechanism for high-mass BBH mergers. Eddington-limited and GRRMHD-informed accretion prescriptions with modest kicks can explain part of the high-mass population, but an additional formation channel is still needed to account for the high fraction of negative χ_eff systems and high secondary BH spins observed in gravitational-wave data.

title: Bipolar HII regions Produced by Cloud-Cloud Collisions
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, 1 table, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We use numerical experiments to explore two possibilities: (i) that Bipolar H II Regions are the result of Cloud-Cloud Collisions (CCCs), and (ii) that -- when allowance is made for the chaotic nature of such collisions, the short duration of the bipolar phase, and different viewing angles -- a large proportion of all H II Regions might be the aftermath of CCCs. To reduce the parameter space, our experiments only consider head-on collisions between two $500$ M$_\odot$ clouds, with three different levels of turbulence, and two different collision velocities; the collision velocities define the `collision axis'. In all experiments, OB stars only condense out after a Shock-Compressed Layer has formed (perpendicular to the collision axis), and fragmented to produce a Hub Filament System, with the OB stars forming in the Hub. Ionising radiation from the OB stars excites an H II Region, which tends to expand more rapidly in directions close to the collision axis, and more slowly in directions orthogonal to the collision axis, where it encounters the dense gas of the Shock-Compressed Layer. Consequently, the H II Region may appear bipolar, for a short period during its evolution, if observed at sufficiently large angle to the collision axis. Viewed from smaller angles, the waist appears as a Bright-Rim, similar to conventional approximately spherical H II Regions. Under this circumstance, there are other metrics -- based on the extent of diffuse freefree emission, the velocity dispersion of Radio Recombination Lines, dust emission at mid-infrared wavelengths -- that might indicate the aftermath of a CCC, and establish CCCs as a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.

AI.tldr: Numerical experiments of head-on cloud-cloud collisions (CCCs) between two 500 solar mass clouds (with varying turbulence and collision velocities) show that OB stars form only after a shock-compressed layer fragments into a hub-filament system. The resulting H II region expands faster along the collision axis and slower perpendicular to it, producing a bipolar appearance when viewed at large angles to the collision axis. When viewed from smaller angles, it resembles a conventional spherical H II region with a bright-rimmed waist, but additional diagnostics (diffuse free-free emission, RRL velocity dispersion, MIR dust emission) may reveal the CCC origin, suggesting CCCs could be a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.
AI.motivation: To test whether bipolar H II regions arise from cloud-cloud collisions, and to determine whether a large fraction of all H II regions might be the aftermath of CCCs when accounting for chaotic collisions, short bipolar-phase durations, and viewing angles — potentially establishing CCCs as a dominant high-mass star formation trigger.
AI.method: Numerical experiments of head-on collisions between two 500 solar mass clouds, varying three turbulence levels and two collision velocities. The collision axis is defined by the velocity. OB star formation, H II region evolution, and observational appearance are tracked as functions of viewing angle.
AI.result: OB stars condense only after a shock-compressed layer forms perpendicular to the collision axis and fragments into a hub-filament system, with stars forming in the hub. The H II region expands faster along the collision axis and slower perpendicular to it (due to dense shocked gas), appearing bipolar for a short period when viewed at large angles to the collision axis. At smaller viewing angles, the waist appears as a bright rim, mimicking conventional spherical H II regions.
AI.conclusion: Bipolar H II regions can be produced by CCCs, and many apparently spherical H II regions may also be CCC aftermaths seen from favorable angles. Alternative diagnostics (diffuse free-free emission extent, radio recombination line velocity dispersion, mid-infrared dust emission) may identify CCC signatures, supporting the idea that CCCs are a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.

title: Comparative Periodogram Analysis of 22 Years of Super-Kamiokande Solar $^{8}\mathrm{B}$ Neutrino Data: Classical, Phase-Based, and Information Theoretic Methods
summary: Solar $^8\mathrm{B}$ neutrinos offer a unique probe of solar interior dynamics and neutrino electromagnetic properties. We present a systematic, multi-method periodogram analysis of the 22-year Super-Kamiokande solar neutrino dataset (1996--2018), comparing nine algorithms. Through hierarchical temporal segmentation, we disentangle astrophysical signals from detector systematics. The Generalized Lomb-Scargle (GLS) method provides the most statistically robust detections by correctly handling heteroscedastic uncertainties, whereas classical Lomb-Scargle systematically underestimates significance. The Lafler--Kinman method generally fails, whereas independent algorithms like MHAOV and PDM1 recover consistent periodicities, providing vital cross-validation. In pre-2001 and SK-I data, seven algorithms provide \textit{weak evidence} ($\ln B > 0$) for a $\sim 38.8$ d periodicity. However, this signal is entirely absent in the highest-statistics SK-IV modified flux data, where the Bayes factor decisively favors the null model ($\ln B \ll -5$), indicating it is a transient feature of the early low-statistics era. Conversely, a $\sim 24.3$ d signal in post-2001 raw flux is decisively rejected by the Bayesian framework and vanishes in modified flux, confirming its seasonal systematic origin. Furthermore, no evidence is found for an $\sim 11$-year solar cycle modulation, yielding a stringent amplitude upper limit of $<0.2\%$ of the mean flux. By highlighting the stark contrast between frequentist significance and Bayesian model selection ($\ln B$) in low signal-to-noise regimes, we establish a rigorous, multi-metric best-practice framework for periodicity searches. This work provides a direct methodological blueprint for next-generation observatories like Hyper-Kamiokande and JUNO.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic multi-method periodogram analysis of 22 years of Super-Kamiokande solar neutrino data (1996-2018) using nine algorithms. The GLS method proves most robust; a ~38.8-day periodicity in early low-statistics data is transient and rejected by Bayesian analysis, a ~24.3-day signal is confirmed as seasonal systematics, no ~11-year solar cycle modulation is found (<0.2% amplitude upper limit), and the work establishes a best-practice framework contrasting frequentist and Bayesian significance.
AI.motivation: To rigorously analyze the long-baseline Super-Kamiokande solar neutrino dataset for periodicities using multiple methods, to disentangle genuine astrophysical signals from detector systematics, and to establish a methodological best-practice framework for periodicity searches in low signal-to-noise regimes for future neutrino observatories.
AI.method: The study employs nine periodogram algorithms (including Generalized Lomb-Scargle, classical Lomb-Scargle, Lafler-Kinman, MHAOV, PDM1) with hierarchical temporal segmentation to separate astrophysical signals from detector systematics. Both frequentist significance and Bayesian model selection (Bayes factor ln B) are used to evaluate detected periodicities in the 22-year Super-Kamiokande dataset.
AI.result: The GLS method provides the most statistically robust detections. Seven algorithms find weak evidence (ln B > 0) for ~38.8-day periodicity in pre-2001/SK-I data, but it is absent in highest-statistics SK-IV modified flux data (ln B << -5), indicating a transient artifact. The ~24.3-day signal in post-2001 raw flux is decisively rejected and vanishes in modified flux, confirming seasonal systematics. No ~11-year solar cycle modulation is found, with an amplitude upper limit of <0.2% of mean flux.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a rigorous multi-metric framework combining frequentist and Bayesian approaches for periodicity searches, demonstrates the critical importance of Bayesian model selection over frequentist significance alone in low signal-to-noise regimes, and provides a methodological blueprint for next-generation observatories such as Hyper-Kamiokande and JUNO.

title: Searching in HI for Massive Low Surface Brightness Galaxies: II. Completing the UGC Sample
summary: Although Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies are increasingly well studied, considerable uncertainty still exists as to both their range in properties and their evolutionary history. LSB galaxies provide a fascinating extreme in galaxy formation and evolution, allowing excellent tests of galaxy formation and evolution theories. Previously, our group successfully measured the HI gas and dynamical mass properties of 350 LSB galaxies, significantly increasing the number of known extreme LSB galaxies (massive, gas rich, etc.) in the process. Here we oresent 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope 21-cm HI line observations of a further 35 LBG galaxies, only two of which have previously published data. Of the 35, 19 were detected. This paper also includes the HI information for five additional galaxies detected accidentally (in the blank sky region or at alternative velocities), none of which has previously published HI results.

AI.tldr: The paper presents new 100-m Green Bank Telescope 21-cm HI line observations of 35 Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies, detecting 19 of them, plus HI data for 5 additional galaxies accidentally detected. This extends the group's previously published sample of 350 LSB galaxies with HI gas and dynamical mass measurements.
AI.motivation: To further characterize the range of properties and evolutionary history of LSB galaxies, which serve as excellent tests of galaxy formation and evolution theories due to their extreme nature.
AI.method: 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope 21-cm HI line observations of 35 LSB galaxies, only two of which had previously published data. Additional HI observations were obtained for 5 galaxies detected serendipitously.
AI.result: 19 of the 35 targeted LSB galaxies were detected in HI, and 5 additional accidental detections were made (in blank sky regions or at alternative velocities), none of which had previously published HI results.
AI.conclusion: This dataset further increases the number of known extreme LSB galaxies (e.g., massive, gas-rich systems), complementing the earlier sample of 350 galaxies and enabling improved statistical studies of LSB galaxy properties and evolution.

title: Impact of Kaon Condensation on the Thermal Evolution of the CCO in HESS J1731--347 Supernova Remnant
summary: Recent analyses of the central compact object in the HESS J1731--347 supernova remnant suggest an unusual combination of a low mass and small radius, while its thermal emission indicates a relatively high surface temperature at its estimated age. Reconciling these structural and thermal properties within a unified theoretical framework may provide important constraints on the equation of state and composition of dense matter. In this work, we investigate the thermal consequences of negatively charged kaon condensation, an exotic phase that softens the equation of state and facilitate the reproduction of the inferred bulk properties of HESS J1731--347. We find that the onset of kaon condensation strongly accelerates the thermal evolution, leading to surface temperature substantially below the observationally inferred range. Within the adopted cooling framework, kaon condensation therefore cannot simultaneously account for the structural and thermal properties of HESS J1731--347.

AI.tldr: The authors investigate whether negatively charged kaon condensation can simultaneously explain both the unusual structural properties (low mass, small radius) and high surface temperature of the central compact object in the HESS J1731--347 supernova remnant. They find that kaon condensation accelerates thermal evolution so strongly that the predicted surface temperature falls well below observed values, ruling it out within their cooling framework.
AI.motivation: The central compact object in HESS J1731--347 exhibits an unusual combination of low mass, small radius, and high surface temperature for its estimated age, which together could constrain the equation of state and composition of dense matter. Reconciling these structural and thermal properties within a unified theory is important for understanding dense matter physics.
AI.method: The authors compute the thermal evolution of neutron stars incorporating negatively charged kaon condensation as an exotic phase that softens the equation of state, then compare the predicted surface temperatures with the observationally inferred range for HESS J1731--347.
AI.result: The onset of kaon condensation strongly accelerates the thermal evolution, producing surface temperatures substantially below the observationally inferred range. Thus, within the adopted cooling framework, kaon condensation cannot simultaneously reproduce the structural and thermal properties of HESS J1731--347.
AI.conclusion: Kaon condensation is ruled out as a unified explanation for the bulk and thermal properties of HESS J1731--347 in the adopted cooling framework, meaning either a different exotic phase, different cooling mechanisms, or revised observational constraints are needed.

title: JWST's Constraints on the Substellar IMF in NGC 2024
summary: A recent study has reported the detection of a turnover in the initial mass function (IMF) below 12 Mjup and the possible detection of a minimum mass near 3 Mjup in the heavily embedded cluster NGC 2024 (<1 Myr), which was based on a sample of brown dwarf candidates in NIRCam images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). I have used those NIRCam data in conjunction with archival spectra from JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) to constrain the substellar IMF in NGC 2024. I present NIRSpec data for 87 sources, 67 of which are within the NIRCam field. Based on those spectra and data from previous studies (e.g., X-ray emission), I have classified 45 of the NIRSpec targets as members of NGC 2024, 17 of which have spectral types indicative of brown dwarfs (M6.5-L; 13 are within NIRCam). The latter have mass estimates as low as 4 Mjup according to theoretical evolutionary models. There remain a few photometric candidates lacking spectra that extend down to the completeness limit of the images (>=2 Mjup for Ak>=1), so the minimum mass of the IMF has not been detected. It is not possible to measure a reliable substellar IMF from the NIRCam images because of the small number of brown dwarfs encompassed by them, a bias against objects at lower masses due to the high extinctions, and incompleteness at >=10 Mjup due to the saturation limit. Thus, there is no evidence in the JWST data for a turnover below 12jup.

AI.tldr: This paper re-analyzes the substellar initial mass function (IMF) in the young cluster NGC 2024 using JWST NIRSpec spectra of 87 sources (67 within the NIRCam field), classifying 45 as cluster members and identifying 17 brown dwarfs (M6.5-L), with masses as low as 4 Mjup. The author concludes that the IMF minimum and a turnover below 12 Mjup cannot be confirmed due to small sample size, extinction bias, and saturation incompleteness.
AI.motivation: A prior study claimed to have detected an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup and a possible minimum mass near 3 Mjup in NGC 2024 based solely on NIRCam imaging. This work aims to test those claims using spectroscopic follow-up with JWST NIRSpec, which provides more reliable member classification and mass constraints than photometry alone.
AI.method: The author combines existing JWST NIRCam imaging with archival NIRSpec spectra for 87 sources (67 within the NIRCam field). Individual sources are classified as cluster members using spectral data combined with prior information such as X-ray emission. Spectral types are converted to masses using theoretical evolutionary models.
AI.result: 45 targets are confirmed as NGC 2024 members, 17 of which are brown dwarfs (spectral types M6.5-L; 13 within NIRCam), with masses as low as 4 Mjup. A few photometric candidates without spectra extend down to the completeness limit (>=2 Mjup). The number of brown dwarfs is too small to derive a reliable substellar IMF, with biases from high extinction against low-mass objects and incompleteness at >=10 Mjup due to saturation.
AI.conclusion: There is no evidence in the JWST data for an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup, and the minimum mass of the IMF has not been detected in NGC 2024. The claims from the earlier photometric study are not supported by the spectroscopic results.

title: The First Measurement of Jet Collimation Profiles in an X-ray Binary: the Case of SS 433
comment: This is a revised manuscript submitted to ApJL
summary: While significant progress has been achieved in active galactic nuclei (AGN), jet collimation profiles in X-ray binaries (XRBs) have not been directly measured. Here we report the first measurement of jet collimation profiles in an XRB using very long baseline interferometry data from SS 433. The approaching jet exhibits a well-constrained quasi-parabolic profile in the 1995 and 1998 data, whereas the prominent local oscillations present in the 2000 jet-width measurements preclude a robust characterization of the jet collimation profile. Nevertheless, the 2000 data suggest that the intrinsic jet opening angle decreases gradually from $\sim 20^\circ$ at 8$\times 10^{14}$ cm to $\sim 3^\circ$ at $9\times 10^{15}$ cm (deprojected), providing evidence for progressive jet collimation. The width and opening angle of the receding jet are also presented, although their interpretation is limited by the free--free absorption effect. In addition, we measure the frequency-dependent core positions at four bands and derive a core-shift relation. These results establish SS 433 as the first XRB in which jet collimation, opening-angle evolution, and core-shift relation are constrained.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first direct measurement of jet collimation profiles in an X-ray binary (XRB) using VLBI data from SS 433. The approaching jet shows a quasi-parabolic profile in 1995/1998 data, while 2000 data reveal a gradual decrease in intrinsic opening angle from ~20° to ~3° over distance, providing evidence for progressive jet collimation. The authors also measure frequency-dependent core positions and derive a core-shift relation.
AI.motivation: While jet collimation profiles have been well-studied in active galactic nuclei (AGN), such profiles have never been directly measured in X-ray binaries (XRBs). Measuring these profiles is crucial for understanding jet physics and comparing jet properties across different scales and source classes.
AI.method: Very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations of the XRB SS 433, analyzing jet-width measurements from three epochs (1995, 1998, and 2000) to characterize the jet collimation profile. The 2000 data were used to track the intrinsic opening angle evolution with deprojected distance, and multi-frequency core positions were analyzed to derive a core-shift relation.
AI.result: The approaching jet exhibits a well-constrained quasi-parabolic profile in 1995 and 1998 data. The 2000 data (though with oscillations precluding robust characterization) suggest the intrinsic jet opening angle decreases from ~20° at 8×10^14 cm to ~3° at 9×10^15 cm, providing evidence for progressive jet collimation. Receding jet width/opening angle are presented but limited by free-free absorption. A core-shift relation was derived from four frequency bands.
AI.conclusion: SS 433 is established as the first X-ray binary in which jet collimation, opening-angle evolution, and core-shift relation are all constrained, bridging the understanding of jet physics between AGN and XRBs.

title: X-ray Absorption Variability in NGC 1142: Another Constraint on the Nature of the Torus/Broad-Line Region in Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: The physics, geometry, and kinematics of the gas and dust surrounding the central engine of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are not well understood. In some sources, this material obscures the coronal X-ray emission, allowing its line-of-sight column density ($N_H$) to be measured. Many sources display $N_H$ variability across multiple epochs. Studying this variability can provide information about the distribution and dynamics of the obscuring material. Particularly, previous works have shown that the probability of observing $N_H$ variability increases with the number of observations available. Additionally, the observed magnitudes of the $N_H$ variability depend on the timescale between observations. In this work, we present the $N_H$ variability analysis of NGC 1142, which has a total of nine X-ray observations over $\sim20$ years, including five from a NuSTAR+XMM-Newton monitoring campaign performed in 2024-2025 and reported here for the first time. We use the physically-motivated torus models UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, and RXTorusD to model the spectra. Our results confirm the previously observed trends, and we compare these trends to simulated obscuration curves assuming different locations and distributions of obscuring clouds.

AI.motivation: The distribution and dynamics of obscuring material around AGN central engines are poorly understood. Studying N_H variability across multiple epochs can provide insights into the physical geometry and kinematics of this gas and dust, helping to constrain the nature of the obscuring torus.
AI.method: The authors present N_H variability analysis for NGC 1142 using nine X-ray observations over ~20 years. Five of these come from a new NuSTAR+XMM-Newton monitoring campaign (2024-2025). Spectra were modeled with physically-motivated torus models including UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, and RXTorusD. Results were compared to simulated obscuration curves assuming different cloud locations and distributions.

These trends were compared to simulated obscuration curves for different cloud configurations.

title: Multiwavelength study of supernova remnants in the Circinus constellation with SRG/eROSITA
summary: Supernova remnants (SNRs) are key tracers of stellar feedback and the chemical and dynamical evolution of the interstellar medium. However, identifying SNRs in complex regions remains challenging, particularly when only archival multi-wavelength data are available. We aim to search for previously unrecognized SNR candidates in the Circinus constellation by combining optical imaging, radio continuum data, and available SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey X-ray observations, to provide a prioritized list of targets for future confirmation. Candidate remnants were classified according to the strength of the combined diagnostics. This joint analysis yields improved constraints on the morphology and spectral properties of known remnants in the region, including MSH 15-52 and G320.6- 1.6. In addition, we identify a new promising SNR candidate, G320.2-3.6. Our study provides a first multi-wavelength search of SNR candidates in the Circinus region. In addition to G320.2-3.6, three objects (G319.8-2.0, G321.8-1.1, and G320.5-1.8) emerge as promising targets for follow-up radio, spectroscopic optical, and deeper, spatially resolved X-ray observations to confirm their nature.

AI.tldr: A multi-wavelength search combining optical, radio, and X-ray (eROSITA) data identifies new supernova remnant (SNR) candidates in the Circinus constellation, including a promising new candidate G320.2-3.6 and three other targets for follow-up confirmation.
AI.motivation: Identifying supernova remnants in complex regions is challenging, especially when only archival multi-wavelength data are available. The authors aim to search for previously unrecognized SNR candidates in the Circinus constellation using combined optical, radio, and X-ray observations.
AI.method: The authors combine optical imaging, radio continuum data, and SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey X-ray observations to search for SNR candidates. Candidate remnants are classified according to the strength of combined multi-wavelength diagnostics.
AI.result: The joint analysis provides improved constraints on known remnants in the region (MSH 15-52 and G320.6-1.6) and identifies a new promising SNR candidate, G320.2-3.6. Three additional objects (G319.8-2.0, G321.8-1.1, and G320.5-1.8) emerge as promising targets for follow-up observations.
AI.conclusion: This study provides the first multi-wavelength search of SNR candidates in the Circinus region, delivering a prioritized list of targets for future radio, spectroscopic optical, and deeper X-ray observations to confirm their SNR nature.

title: Characterizing the disruption of Böotes III: a missing link in the Galactic halo?
summary: The Böotes III (Boo3) dwarf galaxy has long been suspected of being the progenitor of Styx, a ~50°-long stellar stream that was simultaneously discovered in the same region of sky. Boo3's diffuse morphology, large velocity dispersion, small pericenter, and excess of candidate stars at large radii suggest it is undergoing active tidal disruption. A link to Styx is therefore logical; however, a clear connection between these structures has not yet been clearly demonstrated. Here, we re-examine the Boo3-Styx association by searching for Boo3's tidal debris using a combination of Gaia-selected members, new CaHK narrow-band imaging with CFHT/MegaCam, and stellar tracer catalogues of blue horizontal branch and red giant branch stars. We also conduct a broad search for a putative stream using matched filter techniques applied to SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2. Despite our extensive search, we find no observational evidence directly linking Boo3 to Styx. Furthermore, our results suggest that either Boo3's extended substructure is too diffuse to be detected with current data, or that its particular orbit may have erased a coherent tidal signature. Boo3 thus remains an enigmatic system, and exemplifies the need for spectroscopic follow-up to properly disentangle the nature between this faint Milky Way satellite and nearby stream.

AI.tldr: The authors re-examine the suspected association between the Boötes III dwarf galaxy and the Styx stellar stream, but find no observational evidence directly linking them despite extensive searches using Gaia, CFHT/MegaCam CaHK imaging, BHBs/RGBs, and matched filters on SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2. Boo3's extended substructure may be too diffuse to detect or its orbit may have erased a coherent tidal signature.
AI.motivation: Boo3 has long been suspected to be the disrupted progenitor of the ~50°-long Styx stream, but a clear connection has never been demonstrated. Establishing whether Boo3 is actively disrupting and whether Styx is its debris is important for understanding the nature of faint Milky Way satellites and their tidal evolution.
AI.method: The authors combine several datasets: (1) Gaia-selected member stars of Boo3, (2) new CaHK narrow-band imaging from CFHT/MegaCam, (3) stellar tracer catalogues of blue horizontal branch and red giant branch stars, and (4) a broad matched-filter search for a putative stream using SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2 photometry.
AI.result: Despite the extensive multi-wavelength search, no observational evidence is found that directly links Boo3 to Styx. The results suggest either that Boo3's extended tidal substructure is too diffuse to be detected with current data, or that its orbit has erased any coherent tidal signature.
AI.conclusion: Boo3 remains an enigmatic system. The authors emphasize the need for dedicated spectroscopic follow-up to properly disentangle the relationship between this faint Milky Way satellite and the nearby Styx stream.

title: Estimating amplitude of matter density fluctuations in solar and supernova models using neutrino flavor evolution
summary: Neutrinos can undergo substantial flavor evolution between their production in astrophysical sources-such as the Sun and core-collapse supernovae-and their subsequent detection in terrestrial detectors. This flavor evolution is strongly influenced by the environment that the neutrinos interact with, making them useful astrophysical messengers capable of potentially carrying information about the properties of the source wherein they are produced. In this work, we apply the framework of statistical data assimilation (SDA) in order to ascertain the extent to which a neutrino signal at detection may contain information about matter density fluctuations along their path from the source. Using simplified models of neutrino flavor evolution and propagation in the sun and in a core-collapse supernova (CCSN), we find that the SDA method is able to extract information about the amplitude of density fluctuations in both the solar and CCSN scenarios, with the method showing relatively greater reliability in the solar neutrino case. Nonetheless, even in the CCSN neutrino model, the method proved effective at high fluctuation amplitudes

AI.tldr: This paper applies statistical data assimilation (SDA) to determine whether neutrino signals detected on Earth can reveal information about matter density fluctuations along their propagation path from astrophysical sources. Using simplified models of solar and core-collapse supernova (CCSN) neutrinos, the method successfully extracts density fluctuation amplitude information in both scenarios, with greater reliability for solar neutrinos, though CCSN neutrinos remain effective at high fluctuation amplitudes.
AI.motivation: Neutrino flavor evolution is strongly influenced by the environment they traverse, making them potential astrophysical messengers. The authors seek to ascertain the extent to which detected neutrino signals can carry information about matter density fluctuations along their path from the source, addressing a key question about the diagnostic power of neutrinos.
AI.method: The authors apply the framework of statistical data assimilation (SDA) to simplified models of neutrino flavor evolution and propagation in the Sun and in a core-collapse supernova, analyzing how well the method can extract information about the amplitude of density fluctuations from the detected neutrino signal.
AI.result: The SDA method successfully extracts information about density fluctuation amplitudes in both solar and CCSN scenarios. The method demonstrates greater reliability in the solar neutrino case. In the CCSN neutrino model, the method proved effective specifically at high fluctuation amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: Neutrino signals at detection can indeed carry information about matter density fluctuations along their propagation path, and SDA provides a viable framework for extracting this information. However, the reliability depends on the astrophysical scenario—stronger for solar neutrinos and requiring high fluctuation amplitudes for CCSN neutrinos.

title: Binary neutron stars in the next-generation era: Multi-messenger detection prospects and constraints on the equation of state, mass distribution, and cosmology
summary: Next-generation gravitational-wave (GW) observatories will provide crucial insights into the nature of neutron star (NS) matter and the cosmological expansion history. We estimate the number of multi-messenger detections from binary neutron stars (BNS) with the Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer (CE), and project the resulting constraints on the equation of state (EOS), BNS mass distribution, and cosmology via joint hierarchical Bayesian inference. Assuming a local merger rate of 106.6 Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$ and considering two different mass functions, a narrow one centred around 1.4 $M_\odot$ and a wide one ranging between 1.1--2 $M_\odot$, we find that for ET, our mock follow-up algorithm results in at least $\sim40$ and up to $\sim100$ successfully identified electromagnetic counterparts per year, depending on the detector layout and mass distribution. In a joint network with CE, the number of multi-messenger detections can range from $\sim 200$ to $\sim500$. Additionally, several more afterglows from gamma-ray bursts or KNe could be found with dedicated late-time observations. Based on the identified multi-messenger events, we perform an injection campaign to hierarchically constrain the EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology in a fully Bayesian framework. Focussing on ET alone, we show how in an ideal scenario, GW signals, KNe, and host galaxy redshifts can constrain the canonical NS radius $R_{1.4}$ within $\sim 0.2$ km and the Hubble constant $H_0$ within $\sim 1$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, while recovering the essential features of the mass distribution. By comparing inference results that rely solely on GW data and those that incorporate light curve information, we find that while KN light-curve posteriors have a negligible impact on the EOS constraints, they can benefit the inference of cosmological parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper projects multi-messenger detection rates of binary neutron star mergers with next-generation gravitational wave observatories (Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer), and uses simulated multi-messenger events to constrain the neutron star equation of state, BNS mass distribution, and cosmology through joint hierarchical Bayesian inference.
AI.motivation: Next-generation GW observatories will detect many BNS mergers, providing opportunities to constrain NS matter properties, mass distribution, and cosmology through multi-messenger observations. The paper aims to quantify the expected yields and achievable precision.
AI.method: The authors estimate multi-messenger detection rates for ET and CE using mock follow-up algorithms, assuming a local merger rate of 106.6 Gpc^-3 yr^-1 and two mass functions (narrow around 1.4 M_sun and wide spanning 1.1-2 M_sun). They then perform an injection campaign for joint hierarchical Bayesian inference combining GW signals, kilonova light curves, and host galaxy redshifts to constrain EOS, mass distribution, and H0.
AI.result: ET alone yields ~40-100 EM counterparts per year depending on detector layout and mass distribution; with CE in a network, 200-500 multi-messenger detections per year. In an ideal scenario, the canonical NS radius R_1.4 can be constrained to ~0.2 km and H0 to ~1 km/s/Mpc. KN light-curve data has negligible impact on EOS constraints but benefits cosmological parameter inference.
AI.conclusion: Next-generation GW observatories will provide large multi-messenger BNS samples enabling precise constraints on NS EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology, with kilonova information primarily aiding cosmological inference rather than EOS measurements.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Tidal Disruption Event Classification : A Host-Agnostic Probabilistic Random Forest Approach
summary: The classification of Tidal Disruption Events in large-scale photometric surveys is challenging because deterministic machine learning models produce overconfident misclassifications under varying data quality and low signal-to-noise conditions. Existing lightcurve-based approaches fail to incorporate measurement uncertainties, consequently generating brittle outputs. We present a host-agnostic, uncertainty-aware classification framework using a Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF). Our pipeline extracts 11 characteristic features from nuclear transients in the ZTF alert stream, including rise and decay timescales, blackbody temperature evolution, and pre-transient variability metrics. Relying exclusively on photometric data without host galaxy information ensures effectiveness for the faint transient population expected from the Rubin Observatory. The PRF, which treats feature measurements as distributions, was evaluated against XGBoost through Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation. It yields higher stability and robustness for ambiguous candidates than XGBoost. The two classifiers occupy complementary regimes. XGBoost achieves higher recall in balanced and high-precision scenarios, where its rigid decision boundaries efficiently isolate TDE-like sources, while PRF rejects more false positives by penalizing sources with large feature uncertainties. Applying this framework to archival data identified 11 new candidate TDEs from the unclassified population and 3 potential photometric TDEs within existing training labels previously misclassified as supernovae or active galactic nuclei. This work demonstrates that TDEs can be reliably identified using photometric lightcurve features, providing a host-independent framework. Uncertainty-aware, probabilistic classifiers are essential for the Rubin era to prevent the overconfident misclassifications inherent in deterministic models at low signal-to-noise.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a host-agnostic, uncertainty-aware Tidal Disruption Event (TDE) classification framework using a Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF). The pipeline extracts 11 photometric features from ZTF alert stream data and treats feature measurements as distributions rather than point values. Compared to XGBoost via Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation, the PRF shows higher stability and robustness for ambiguous candidates, rejects more false positives under uncertainty, and identified 11 new candidate TDEs plus 3 reclassified photometric TDEs from archival data.
AI.motivation: Deterministic machine learning models for TDE classification in large-scale photometric surveys produce overconfident misclassifications under varying data quality and low signal-to-noise conditions. Existing lightcurve-based approaches fail to incorporate measurement uncertainties, resulting in brittle outputs. A robust, uncertainty-aware classification method is needed for the faint transient population expected from the Rubin Observatory.
AI.method: The authors propose a Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF) classifier that treats feature measurements as distributions instead of point values. The pipeline extracts 11 characteristic features from nuclear transients in the ZTF alert stream—including rise/decay timescales, blackbody temperature evolution, and pre-transient variability metrics—using exclusively photometric data without host galaxy information.
